doc.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Joe Williams's stage presence and Tony Bennett's transformation
summary: Williams wanted to be a ballad singer; Crow tells how Mitch Miller shaped Tony Bennett and how Basie's band changed him.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Joe Williams: the singer with Basie

blocks.x: Yeah, oh, yeah. So Joe was very well supported by those arrangements. They really, and he knew what to do with them. He had an instrument and an ability to sing and actually he was kind of bugged about getting locked into the image of being a blues singer, because he wanted to be a ballad singer. And he knew he could do it, and he felt that he had come into the world of being a singer kind of on the tail end of the time when those kind of singers were easily promoted and sold to the general public. So you know he was glad to have the gig with a major band but he really hated the fact that all he got to do was these three or four blues charts that Basie had for him. And Basie could see what an impact he was having on the audience, you know. I mean and it was only about his voice. Because at that time he had no stage presence at all. You know he had a bad haircut, it was shaved way up to the top of his head, and he had a jacket that was too short for him, and he would just come out and hold his hands like this and close his eyes and sing. And made very little eye contact with the audience you know. But I mean it was dynamite. Everybody would just fall all over themselves and so became a star immediately. It wasn’t too long that he loosened up and started to play to audiences, got a better tailor, got a better barber. And by the time that band had been coming through there for a couple, three years, Joe had really turned into a — well it’s very much like what happened to Tony Bennett. The first time I heard Tony I was over at Jack Segal’s house, the songwriter that wrote “When Sunny Gets Blue” and “Scarlet Ribbons” and some of those songs. And Jack was busy in the Brill Building world, he knew people and he knew songwriters, and he was always good for a dinner and a loan of $5 if I would go over there scuffling. And he was a nice guy, and we always had parties at his house. And we would do things like sit around reading Clifford Odets’ plays or singing. It was very entertainment oriented happening over at his house. And one time I was over there and this guy brings Tony Bennett by and says, “I want you to hear this young singer I got and see what you think.” And he was kind of a straight, not jazz oriented singer at all, not even pop jazz oriented. He was singing like an Eddie Fisher type of singer. And he sang a little flat on his high notes, and he was singing loud, full, like out of the Milanese pop song style, almost operatic you know, except he didn’t make those operatic noises that opera singers do. And the next thing we knew, somebody had gotten him, well it was mob connections, they had gotten him a record contract with Columbia, and they gave Mitch Miller the job of promoting him. And Mitch realized that he had an interesting anguished sound in his upper register, so he deliberately put him a key or two higher than he really was comfortable singing, and then he’d have him do eight or ten takes until he really sounded like he was dying and there were songs about mama and love and all of that, and he gave it an emotional quality that Mitch knew was marketable. So he got popular enough, and you know Tony was a darling guy, just a really, everybody liked © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

him he was such a nice man, and kind of innocent. And I just heard this on the grapevine, I never discussed it with Tony, but I heard that he bought his contract away from these guys that originally backed him, and they charged him a nice taste, but they were willing to let him go because he was a nice guy. And then I think it was either hearing the Basie band or getting a chance to work opposite the Basie band, he realized that that was the kind of the background he would like to hear behind him. He liked it. And also the first time that he got out with a supper club audience, he fell in love with audiences. It turns out that he had this ability to really relate to people in a very personal way as a performer. And it just changed him completely. He became an entirely different singer than he ever had been before. So jazz had a very good influence on him I think. Basie had a good influence.
Yeah. Well he made some marvelous records with Basie too.
